extracted.intended_audience: federal agency rulemaking staff, policymakers, and administrators responsible for managing public comments
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on preserving the integrity and value of the administrative notice-and-comment process in the face of mass, malattributed, and computer-generated public comments, including detection, technological responses, legal considerations, and tools to summarize and analyze comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy of assertions within comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish malattribution (wrong author name) from inaccuracy in the substantive assertions of a comment; commenters (even those using their own names) may misrepresent experiences, expertise, or views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The malattribution problem is distinct from accuracy of factual assertions; agencies should be alert that comments under real names can still contain false claims (example: SEC proxy rule proceeding). Detection and response strategies should account for factual accuracy as a separate concern from provenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight of public support or opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether mass or malattributed comments mislead the agency about public sentiment by creating the appearance of many distinct individuals commenting when a single actor produced the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how identical or near-identical comments attached to many names may be perceived as broad public sentiment (Net Neutrality example). Agencies should evaluate whether apparent volume or multiplicity of identities affects decisionmaking and whether different presentation (e.g., anonymous vs purportedly distinct names) changes perceived credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harms to individuals from malattribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize psychological and reputational harms to people whose names/emails are used without permission in comments; harms may be real though sometimes hard to quantify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Victims may be annoyed, distressed, or suffer reputational damage (e.g., viral attention). Agencies should consider potential harms even if not amounting to statutory identity theft, and weigh options such as removal of fraudulent comments or notifying authorities when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: User notice and legal deterrence
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide clear Terms of Participation that warn users that knowingly making materially false or fraudulent statements about identity in comments may violate federal law (e.g., 18 U.S.C. §1001; §1028).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations.gov includes a user notice that by submitting a comment the user verifies they are not making materially false statements about identity. Such notices may deter some individual misuse but are unlikely to stop large-scale automated operations; placement and visibility of the notice matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency protocols for handling malattributed comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish policies and procedures for how to resolve suspected malattributed comments, including whether to investigate provenance, flag comments, or assist in criminal investigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many agencies lack protocols. Policies should address whether staff should attempt to resolve provenance or simply flag potential malattribution, and whether staff/resources will be provided to assist law enforcement if prosecution is considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentication technologies to verify commenter identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider technological methods to authenticate commenters, such as secure login, two-factor authentication, biometric checks, security questions, or name verification against databases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These technologies exist and are widely used elsewhere but are not currently implemented to the degree of, e.g., driver's-license-level authentication. Agencies should weigh technical feasibility against policy goals (noting tension with anonymous commenting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of human/bot verification tools (CAPTCHA/reCAPTCHA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deploy Turing-test-style tools (CAPTCHA, reCAPTCHA) to distinguish automated bots from human commenters and impose a 'speed bump' in the commenting process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: reCAPTCHA v3 uses risk analysis to assign scores and flag suspicious activity; these tools can reduce automated submissions but are imperfect (can be defeated) and may not stop sophisticated operations. They may also reduce some malattributed activity by making mass submission harder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorized-entity API posting with identity validation
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow verified entities to post mass comment campaigns via an API after verification by a government authority using commercial identity-validation services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations.gov's API permits authorized entities verified by GSA to post mass campaigns; the service is designed to assure entities 'are who they say they are' but does not verify individual commenters. Agencies should consider how such arrangements affect transparency and provenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tension between authentication and anonymity
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that front-end identity authentication conflicts with longstanding policies allowing anonymous public comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must balance integrity of the docket against the right to submit anonymously; any move toward authentication will require policy choices about preserving anonymity and access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to consider substantive issues regardless of source
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the APA, agencies must consider and respond to significant issues raised in comments; the source (computer-generated or not) does not automatically remove that obligation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if comments are computer-generated, agencies should evaluate whether they present unique, significant issues requiring response. In litigation, courts may consider the reliability/authenticity of comments when assessing claims that agencies failed to consider relevant issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: De-duplication as mass comment management
rubrics_metrics.description: Use de-duplication software to identify and group identical or near-duplicate comments, isolating unique substantive content for agency review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies commonly treat mass and some computer-generated comments as a de-duplication problem; deduping can reveal unique content among many similar submissions and reduce reviewer burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual indicators for identifying computer-generated comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Look for textual 'tells' such as repeated phrases, search-and-replace permutations, unusual brevity, repeated grammatical errors, nonsensical strings, or phrase combinations that recur with substitutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses of net neutrality comments found recurring sentence templates with substituted tokens (e.g., 'Americans' replaced by 'people like me'). Shorter comments provide fewer 'tells'; longer comments yield more signals for detection. Use pattern-search methods to find such fingerprints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal and metadata indicators for identifying computer-generated comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine timing and metadata patterns: large numbers of submissions at the same second, periodic on/off submission cycles, repetition of email domains, improbable or uniform name/address/email formatting, and lack of email confirmation requests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FCC analyses found hundreds of thousands of emails from the same address ranges and many submissions occurring at identical timestamps. Such anomalous metadata can be a strong signal of automated or centralized generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators in auxiliary fields (names, addresses, emails)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess consistency/uniformity in non-text fields (name, address, email) as evidence of automation: unusually complete/consistent entries, inability of email addresses to receive messages, or concentrations in particular domains/countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human-entered metadata is typically varied and inconsistent; highly uniform or systematically patterned auxiliary fields suggest algorithmic generation or one-off email providers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and resource tradeoffs in detection
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge that systematic identification of computer-generated comments is resource-intensive and agencies may prioritize analysis of substantive issues over provenance detection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interviews indicated agencies often do not prioritize bot-detection because of bandwidth constraints; detection requires substantial effort and may divert resources from evaluating substantive, significant comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk monitoring for future technological threats
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuously monitor advances in text generation and related technologies to assess whether detection will become impractical and whether legitimacy of the notice-and-comment process is threatened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technologists warn that future models may mimic humans so closely detection becomes impossible; agencies should plan monitoring and contingencies to preserve meaningful participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of NLP summarization to enhance comment review
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply natural language processing (NLP) tools to summarize, sort, and extract the most relevant substantive information from large comment corpora to assist rulewriters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NLP can identify parts of comments that relate to specific regulatory questions, legal or technical information, and patterns across comments. Agencies may deploy summarization and topic-modeling to save time and improve analysis, especially for high-volume rulemakings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific NLP tools and metrics for comment analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider employing tools/metrics such as Flesch–Kincaid readability, LIWC (psychology-relevant word categories), plagiarism/similarity detection, automated document summarization, sentiment analysis, topic modeling, and word embeddings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each technique serves different analytic purposes: readability measures clarity; LIWC tracks psychological signals; plagiarism detection finds textual overlap; summarizers condense content; sentiment analysis estimates valence; topic models extract latent themes; embeddings capture semantic relationships. Use combinations appropriate to the task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine automation with human oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Use mixed human–machine workflows where algorithms do initial sorting/summarization and humans validate, refine, and ensure accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include the State Department passport engagement where machine summaries were proofed and edited by humans. Human oversight can correct domain-specific errors, retrain models, and confirm reliability—making semi-automated approaches more trustworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model retraining and domain adaptation for important rulemakings
rubrics_metrics.description: Invest in retraining NLP models on domain-specific language when necessary for high-profile or complex rulemakings to improve accuracy and relevance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Domain-specific jargon may require retraining models; for important rulemakings expected to receive many comments, the investment in retraining may be justified to improve summarization and extraction performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding wrongful exclusion when using detection/authentication
rubrics_metrics.description: Design detection or authentication systems so they do not unintentionally exclude legitimate comments—especially those that raise unique significant issues—simply because of source or algorithmic flags.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technology that filters or denies comments could prevent agencies from receiving novel substantive input; any screening must account for the APA obligation to consider significant issues and include safeguards (e.g., human review of flagged items).
